title: Orla and the Missing Picnic
markdown:
In the far green peaks of Bramblehorn, where the clouds often wore silly hats and the wind sang lullabies to sleeping toadstools, lived a young witch named Orla. Her hair was the colour of the deepest twilight, and her spells, still learning their full might, were always brewed with the finest intentions. Her dearest companion was a hedgehog named Pip. Pip’s quills were as neatly placed as a knight’s armour, and his favourite pastime was ensuring everything was precisely where it ought to be. It was a perfectly ordinary Tuesday, which, in Bramblehorn, meant it was quite extraordinary.

“Pip, my dear fellow,” Orla announced, voice like the chime of tiny silver bells, “the sunbeams are at their most golden, and the dewdrop tarts are just cooling. It is a perfect time for a picnic.” The air hummed with anticipation and the faint sweet scent of wild thyme.

Pip, who had already arranged the checkered blanket into a series of perfect squares, gave a pleased little huff. Whiskers twitched. “Indeed, Orla. The cucumber sandwiches are cut into triangles, precisely three per person. The berry cordial is chilled to just the right temperature. And the cheese is sliced with nary a crumb out of place. Everything is just so.” He smoothed a stray quill with his tiny paw. Pip believed a picnic, like a perfectly ironed shirt, was ruined by even a single crease out of place.

Orla’s smile broadened, a genuine sunlit thing. She reached for the wicker basket, woven from moonlit willow and smelling faintly of lavender and warm honey. It was usually right there, beside the carefully arranged forget-me-nots. Her hand met empty air. A cold fluttery sensation rippled through her heart. Breath caught. A tightness bloomed in her chest. The silver bells of her voice tarnished a shade. “Pip. Have you seen the picnic basket?”

Pip’s neat spines bristled, a most un-Pip-like occurrence. He scurried, nose twitching frantically. “It was here, Orla. Beside the lavender bunches. Unthinkable. Utterly, completely, unbelievably absent.” A small distressed squeak.

The basket that held all their yummy treats was gone. As the last rays of golden sun began to stretch long dancing shadows across the meadow, Orla knew they must seek it. The gentle breeze that had been whispering through the tall grass now seemed to sigh. “We shall venture into the Whispering Woods,” she declared, trying to inject a bravery that felt a little shaky. A tiny seed of what-if: the berry cordial never sipped, Pip’s careful preparations for naught.

The Whispering Woods were deep verdant shadows and colossal trees that leaned in to share secrets, their canopy kissing the sky. Ferns unfurled like sleepy green arms. Thick moss carpeted the ground like an emerald velvet rug and muffled their footsteps. Orla’s eyes scanned shifting light and shadow. Pip’s nose drank in damp earthy scent of decaying leaves and hidden flowers.

Before anything appeared, Orla sat a moment and listened. The woods breathed. A beetle, shell like polished obsidian, crawled across a fallen leaf. The air smelled like rain that had fallen long ago. Pip sat beside her, still and quiet, as if listening too.

Suddenly a series of panicked chirps, like tiny bells clanging in distress, echoed through the trees. From behind a giant mushroom no bigger than a teacup and shaped like a little umbrella tumbled a creature of shimmering scales. A dragonet, no larger than a robin, scales that glittered like a hundred scattered emeralds, catching faint light and sending tiny rainbows dancing on the moss. He flapped frantically, utterly bewildered, small face a picture of dismay.

“Oh, dear,” chirped the dragonet, tinkling slightly out-of-tune bells. “Oh, my apologies. I seem to have caused a bit of a kerfuffle.” He landed with a soft rustle, rather flustered.

Orla, initial worry forgotten in the face of such a marvellous unexpected sight, knelt, twilight hair falling around her shoulders. “A kerfuffle? What kind of kerfuffle?” she asked gently.

The dragonet puffed his tiny chest. “A basket-kerfuffle. I was practising my snatch-and-flit spells, you see, for a game of catch the falling leaf. A very important game for dragonets. But I got a bit enthusiastic. And I might have accidentally snatched a rather lovely basket. It’s very important that it’s returned before the moon fully rises, or the jam might lose its jiggle.” He wrung his tiny claws.

Orla’s worry about jam jiggling was, admittedly, less pressing than an entire picnic disappearing. But the dragonet’s tiny frame shook, emerald eyes wide. His voice trembled. This was Sparkle, whose playful magic often caused a stir in Bramblehorn. Scales shimmered with an inner light, a gentle harmless magic that only sometimes went a little astray. “Don’t fret too much, little one,” Orla said, soft as a warm breeze. “We’re looking for it too. Can you remember where you took it?”

Sparkle wrung his claws again. “It’s a bit muddled. It flew this way, then that way, then I think it did a little dance near the Whispering Willow. And then I got distracted by a particularly sparkly beetle. It had wings like stained glass.” He pointed a small trembling claw vaguely into the deeper woods.

The sun dipped lower, painting the sky in rose and amber, colours bleeding like spilled paint on a celestial canvas. The thought of returning without the basket, without the perfectly cut sandwiches and the chilled cordial, pricked at Orla. Her quiet fear was of things going awry, of not being prepared for the unexpected. She looked at Sparkle, so earnest in his distress, and then at Pip, whose neat spines were beginning to show deep concern; he had nudged her hand once already, a quiet plea.

“Perhaps,” Orla suggested, a thought as tempting as a freshly baked moonbeam cookie, voice tinged with a weariness that surprised even herself, “we could just enchant some new sandwiches. I have a rather excellent spell for turning pebbles into gingerbread. It’s very nearly as good as the real thing.” She took a step toward a pile of smooth grey stones and began to gather them. It would be so much easier to simply make new.

Sparkle’s emerald scales drooped further. “But the berry cordial. It needs the special wicker to keep its sparkle. And the dewdrop tarts, they have to sit just so.” He looked utterly crestfallen.

Orla paused, the allure of an easy magical fix tugging at her. She saw the pebbles glinting, felt the familiar pull of convenience. Pip nudged her hand with his snout again, a silent reminder of the effort that had gone into this specific picnic. Sparkle’s genuine distress was a soft ache in the air, like the distant sound of a sad song. She squared her shoulders. “No,” she said, voice firming, silver bells ringing with renewed clarity. “We will find the real basket. Tell me again, Sparkle. Where did you see the sparkly beetle?”

Sparkle, hopes rekindled, pointed toward a patch of moss that glowed with a soft light seeming to come from within. “Over there. Near the Singing Ferns. And the basket landed with a gentle thump right next to it.”

With Sparkle guiding them, flitting ahead like a tiny dazzling jewel leaving a trail of faint emerald dust, Orla and Pip followed. They scrambled over gnarled roots that snaked like sleeping dragons and ducked beneath dripping branches, the quest leading them deeper. The air grew cooler, richer with damp earth and unseen wildflowers. At last they reached a small clearing bathed in the soft otherworldly glow of the luminous moss. There, nestled beside a cluster of ferns that hummed a soft melodic tune, as if sharing a quiet secret, was their picnic basket, perfectly intact. A sigh of immense relief escaped Orla, warm and deep.

But as they approached, Sparkle let out a little whimper, glittering scales dimming slightly in the twilight. “Oh, dear. Now I’ve got to get home. My Mama worries terribly if I’m out after twilight. But the path is quite dark, and my light only lasts so long before it needs a rest.” His tiny voice trembled.

Orla looked at Sparkle’s small flickering glow. She knew what she had to do. She reached into her pouch and pulled out her most treasured possession: a single shimmering dewdrop charm. It pulsed with a gentle steady light, cool and smooth against her palm, smelling faintly of dawn mist. This light could banish even the deepest shadow, a secret comfort on dark nights. With a deep breath she held it out.

“Here, Sparkle,” she said, warm and steady. “This will light your way home. It’s very precious to me, but your mama will be so relieved to see you safe.” The air thickened, humming with a soft magic that felt both ancient and new. The charm pulsed, unwavering. She offered what she held dear, not out of obligation, but because the little dragonet needed the path more than she needed the night-light.

Sparkle’s eyes widened, then filled with a shimmering gratitude that outshone his emerald scales. “Oh, Orla. Thank you. This is too kind.” He carefully took the charm. Its light immediately illuminated the path ahead, a warm inviting glow through the darkening woods. With a final bell-like chirp of thanks, so clear and bright it seemed to chase away the shadows, Sparkle flitted away, a tiny beacon disappearing into the deepening forest.

Orla and Pip watched him go. A quiet satisfaction settled, warmer than any sunbeam. The sun had slipped below the horizon, leaving deep indigo scattered with the first faint pinpricks of starlight. The woods were no longer daunting. They held a peaceful stillness.

Back at their cozy cottage, with the dewdrop charm safely illuminating Sparkle’s journey, Orla and Pip laid out their rescued picnic. It was not quite the same as it would have been under the golden afternoon sun. The sandwiches were a little cooler, the cordial perhaps a touch less chilled, and the dewdrop tarts had lost some of their morning shimmer. But as Orla offered Pip a perfectly triangular cucumber sandwich, her smile was brighter than before, a steady confident light.

“Well, Pip,” she said, a hint of amusement, “that was certainly an adventure. We didn’t quite have the picnic I planned, but it was, in its own way, quite delightful.” She gazed out at the newly risen moon, a silver disc hanging like a pearl. No melancholy. Only a quiet contentment. The day had been unexpected, a little wobbly, and certainly not perfect. They ate the cooler sandwiches anyway, and the cordial still tasted of berries, and Pip, after a moment of considering the slightly less chilled cheese, restored one corner of the blanket to a perfect square and then, for once, left the rest alone.
